utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. On behalf of the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis along with Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And I believe the Usher has gone to fetch the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Pejic. Before Mr. Zecevic resumes his cross-examination, I remind you you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pejic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, yesterday during the examination-in-chief by my learned friend Mr. Hannis, on page 12139 and the following of the transcript, you spoke about reports that you received from the SJBs in the territory of the CSB of Sarajevo. If you remember, there was discussion about the reports concerning the participation of the police in combat operations. Do you remember that part?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To several questions put to you by the Prosecution you gave answers, and you even gave an example of the situation in Ilidza concerning the attack on Nedzarici when the police took part in those combat operations. You said that it was mostly pursuant to the direct instructions of the army or the Crisis Staff. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and that's what I said and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, isn't it, if I understood your testimony correctly, that only subsequently did you receive information from the SJBs to the effect that members of that particular SJB took part in combat operations; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That information, if I understood you correctly, and it isn't very clear in the transcript, that information was received by you at a time when it was possible to communicate it to you and the CSB of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If the combat operations had ceased, that is when the attack was stopped and the lines were stable. Only after the cessation of those activities was it possible to compile a complete report about the number of police officers who had taken part in combat, whether or not anybody had been injured or killed and when they had returned to their SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Only upon the receipt of such a report from the SJB, you, and when I say "you" I mean the CSB, informed the ministry about that in your daily report; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I'm about to show you P625, which is an annual report of the MUP of the RS, in particular, page 32 in e-court, in the Serbian language, which -- which is marked FI21 -- correction, FI20-1307. I'm not sure of the page number in English that's why I gave the ERN number. You remember that yesterday we spoke about the average number of dispatches which in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH, you had at the CSB of Sarajevo in 1992 and 1991. We then mentioned the number of 300.000 dispatches in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH, namely, their communications centre, and you agreed that this number was probably realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think the correct page in e-court for the English is page 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read out the ERN number --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's page 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Let the record show that Mr. Cvijetic joined the Stanisic Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to the question. We had to find the English page number in this document. You remember what was said yesterday about the number of 300.000 dispatches open or sealed in the communications centre of the MUP of the RS [as interpreted] and you agree that this was the approximate number; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the transcript says 300.000 dispatches in the MUP of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was about 300.000 dispatches open and sealed in the communications centre of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BiH before 1992, in peacetime. You see the fourth paragraph in this document which speaks about the total number of dispatches in the communications centre of the MUP of the RS. Can you see it on this page? It's the fourth paragraph in Serbian and the second in English. There are the figures of 4170 and 4400?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the total number of dispatches in nine months was 8.570. Now, such a small number of dispatches certainly is not the result of the absence of security-relevant events; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I wasn't quite sure of the time span in which these 8.000 dispatches were --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- sent back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This report, the P625, covers the period from April until December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So nine months, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Great, thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The whole existence of the MUP RS during the 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is beyond doubt that from April through December 1992, there was a huge number of security-relevant events; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation changed hourly, especially in the early days of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that one of the most important reasons for such a small number of dispatches during that nine-month period, that is, during the war in 1992, is caused by communications problems. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We didn't have enough personnel or equipment. There were no appropriate means of communications that the MUP of the RS could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a fact, isn't it, Mr. Pejic, that after 1992, that is, in 1993, 1994, 1995, the number of dispatches rose significantly in the communications centre of the CSB where you worked and in the entire MUP of the RS; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were manned and we received technical equipment, and as a result, not only the number of dispatches but the amount of communications overall rose too. I believe that in a realistic system appropriate for use in the police, I think that this was actually achieved at sometime in 1993. The year 1992 was, as a whole, problem-ridden, because even when we had procured equipment, we were short of personnel. That's why the MUP to organise two training courses for new signalsmen or communication operators, because whoever was left behind the territory that was controlled by the other side could not report to our communications centre, either because they didn't want to or because they didn't let them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's a fact, isn't it, that the communications centre at the Sarajevo CSB where you worked in 1992 had a total of 1.800 received and sent dispatches; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the exact number can be seen in the log-book of incoming and outgoing dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So we can say that this is an average of 200 dispatches per month, and if I remember correctly, that is a volume which in the CSB of Sarajevo, in the Socialist Republic of BiH before the war, that is in peacetime, was the approximate daily number of telegrams; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would have at least 200 dispatches daily on average.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Hannis on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It had to do with the math. I think the log-book shows that the first entry for CSB Sarajevo was sometime in June. So the time period over which those 1.800 were sent would be June through December, rather than April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I believe they had the joint communication centre for MUP RS and the CSB Sarajevo from -- from April until -- until June, and that is why the first 49 entries are -- are MUP RS, and I think if we add that to the -- to the end number of 1.813, we're still in the vicinity of 1.800-something dispatches a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to show you these documents which I commented upon with Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1428. Can we please show it. These are incoming and outgoing dispatches. In the time period from April through August 1992. [In English] Can -- Mr. Hannis, if you would be so kind to provide the witness with a hard copy of this document. Oh, okay. Thank you very much, Ms. Usher. [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see -- you see, Mr. Pejic, under 3, entry number 3, this is a bulletin of daily events dated 23 April, and it's about one Predrag Mocevic [phoen], his murder and massacre, and among other things, it says that the dispatch was sent to the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To avoid leafing through this document, I'll just read out and you please confirm. Entry number 7, the bulletin dated 24 April was also transmitted to the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The same applies to entry 10, dated 25 April. Equally transmitted to the government.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on the following page, entry 14, entry 18, also to the government.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the log-book says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And so on and so forth. Let us now please look at page 7, entry 30. It's an order about measures, dated 4 May 1992, and in the fourth column to who the dispatch was sent, it says under three, CB Doboj, but there is no phone number nor is it ticked. Tell me, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that the dispatch was not transmitted to the CB of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown page 10, entries 47 and 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 47 is a document entitled "Position on the criteria for determining the reserve police force." The date is the 11th of May, and we can see the list of addressees to whom the dispatch was sent. It says Doboj and Trebinje, but there is no entry made as to the time at which it was sent or reply.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that the dispatches were never sent. Otherwise, there would be a date as well as a number to which it was transmitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the same applies to entry 48.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hope that you will agree with me that this means that the communication lines with the centres in Doboj and Trebinje were nonexistent at this time.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, on the screen, on page 8, line 17, there is an answer registered by the witness in which the witness allegedly said, "This means that the dispatches were never sent." I think this was not the witness's answer, but that was your assumption, is that correct, or did the witness really say so?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honours. I need to find it. Well, I can ask the witness again because I don't think that I made that comment. I asked him open-ended question for his comment, and he said that means that they were not sent at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's just -- let's clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have heard His Honour Judge Harhoff's question. We're looking at entries 47 and 48 where Doboj and Trebinje are listed, and in respect of none of them is there an entry made as to the time or the number to which the dispatch was sent. Can you tell us what this means?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that these two centres did not receive the relevant dispatch from the communications centre. Had they received it, then the manner in which it was transmitted would be recorded, like the telephone number, as well as the time when the dispatch was transmitted. In other words, this dispatch could not have been transmitted from the MUP communications centre. The dispatch had to be sent in a different manner or a courier had to come and pick it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay. So, Mr. Pejic, what the conclusion about these two entries is, if I understand it correctly, is that these two dispatches were at first attempted to be sent by some electronic means but this failed for whatever reason, and so it wasn't sent in the manner in which it had -- was originally foreseen, and failing to send it electronically, your assumption is then that it was sent by some other means, either by courier or otherwise. So is your testimony that the dispatches actually came through to the addressee or to the destinate, or were they never received in the other end? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether these dispatches ever reached Doboj and Trebinje is something that we in the communications centre could not know with any reliability. If they were taken by the couriers who normally did not collect mail in the communications centre, then we wouldn't know of it. Had the courier collected these dispatches in the communications centre itself, then next to these two place names an entry would have been made, taken over by the courier, and his name would normally be written as well as the title of the centre. I suppose that the dispatches were sent to their authors who were also informed of the fact that the dispatches had not been transmitted. I suppose that subsequently a courier could have collected the dispatches either in the minister's office, if the minister was the signatory, or in the office of the authors of the document, or in the office where they were typed up. I don't know if they received it and whether it was a month later, but what I can tell you is that based on the entry in the log-book, they were not transmitted from the communications centre itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pejic, it is a fact, is it not, that all the chiefs of the CSB and the ministry -- ministry in the head office, including the minister, issued instructions to the stations in the field that prompt information should be reported on and that the information sent should be accurate, complete, and exhaustive. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, and this is something that was insisted on on almost a daily basis. I said at the outset that there were employees who were new to the service and who failed to grasp the point or the gist of what security-relevant information is. One of the commanders had not -- had occasion to deal with this sort of information at the post that he held previously in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that as you started giving your testimony this morning, you said that the situation with regard to -- that the situation changed on an hourly basis and that security-relevant information never ceased to reach you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was misinterpreted, my question. My question was the security events -- or, rather, I said first that the situation changed by the hour and that security events and information about these events were numerous.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were engaged in analyses, it is a fact that the news or information received with a delay of one day in war time constitute important information that cannot be utilised in any way anymore. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Any belated information meant that things that had already been done could not be rectified anymore. If an intervention by the police had already ended by that point and if the relevant information was lacking, you find yourself at the end of the day having to remedy the steps taken already rather than directing the activities in the desired way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To illustrate this with an example, I will show you the documents shown to you by Mr. Hannis in his direct examination yesterday. For reference, we're dealing with P1476.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D76. When I said that P1476 is the reference, I meant the reference to the examination by Mr. Hannis, who showed him this document and then proceeded to show him the specific documents appearing in the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see, sir, Mr. Hannis showed you this document yesterday. It's 65 ter 180. It's a MUP dispatch dated the 19th of July, 1992, and its reference number is 10-14/92. Do you recall seeing this document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The document was made as a result of the meeting of the first collegium of the MUP of Republika Srpska held in Belgrade on the 11th of July, 1992, as stated, in fact, in the preamble of the document; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The CSBs are required to send in detailed information about seven different fields, so to speak. One of them is the activity of paramilitary formations, the second is the involvement of the police in combat activities. Perhaps we can turn to page 2. Next, problems related to the prevention and detection of crime and perpetrators thereof; procedures and jurisdiction in the treatment and custody of prisoners, persons evacuated from collection camps into which the army brings Muslim residents without any documents, stating reasons in order to defer such camps that were not defined to the organs of the interior. Next, operation of the military judiciary authorities, et cetera. We will not read it any further, because it's self-explanatory. You see that in the last paragraph the ministry states: "All the data and information shall be submitted by the 25th of July, 1992, at the latest ..."

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As the -- as a result of this dispatch of the MUP that was sent on the 19th of July, your security services centre sent a dispatch which is P1073.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown P1073. Can the witness be shown page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As you see, this is again a document shown to you by my learned friend Mr. Hannis. It bears the reference number 01-127/92. You gave your comments on it because it was mentioned in the log-book of the communications centre. And this is now a letter from the CSB Sarajevo sent to the SJBs out in the field, to their respective chiefs, and bears the date of the 25th of July, 1992. Therein, a request is made for information to be provided on the various issues that the ministry sought from the SJBs. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You see between these two documents, the document that I have shown you a moment ago from the ministry and the document that you're looking at right now, there is an almost seven-day difference. The ministry document is dated the 19th of July, 1992, and it sets out the time limit for the sending out of information of the 25th of July. And as we can see, this request is sent out to the SJBs out in the field only on the 25th of July. And obviously there is a seven-day interval between the two; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That seven-day gap, I suppose -- or, rather, tell me, do you know how it came about, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can rely on in trying to reply to your question is the log-book of incoming and outgoing dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The log-book shows that on that day there were only three dispatches, and they are our own dispatches. So obviously it couldn't have been received from the MUP on that day. And if I look at number 127, then I see that although it is dated 25 July, it left the centre only on the 27th. In other words, it sat there -- there for two days. If it was received on the 25th by the centre, we took another two days to send it out to all the police stations. Obviously, at that time there were also problems with communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, the Prosecutor showed you a document with which the SJB of Ilijas, pursuant to the request and the instructions received from the CSB, and I'm talking about the document we have just looked at, P1073, where the SJB of Ilijas which acts upon this document and sends out a reply to the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 65 ter 2609.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A minute ago we saw that the CSB on the 27th of July sent dispatches to SJBs.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This reply of the Ilijas SJB is dated 5 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And obviously it says: "Re: Your document strictly confidential 01-127/92 of 25 July 1992." So there's a direct link to the previous document that we commented on; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to enter this dispatch in the log-book of incoming and outgoing dispatches?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is the handwritten number up there, and the Prosecutor asked me about its significance. It means that under 218, the dispatch is entered as received by the communications centre on the 11th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There's again a difference in dates. This document is dated 5 August, and the CSB obviously received it six or seven days later. Do you know the reason why there was this delay?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously at that time communications lines with Ilijas were not functional.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure, but I think that Mr. Hannis tendered this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, it has been confirmed it is an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry, I missed the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is Exhibit P1476, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Pejic. We have given an illustration by using documents in which this is obvious. Let me summarise. From the moment the dispatch was drafted in the ministry and is dated 19 July 1992, the deadline for the submission of information according to that dispatch is 25 July, and we have just seen that the CSB only received information from the SJBs on the 11th of August, which means almost, if my math is correct, almost 21 days --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I object to the form of the question, because he's only shown one being received on the 11th of August, and he says SJBs in the plural in his question. And also, just for clarification, I think in fairness, he should show you what deadline was given to the SJBs in the dispatch from the CSB. It wasn't July 25th. It was August 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree. In the letter sent by the CSB, the deadline was the 10th of August, but I'm interested in the following: Information from the field. The Ilijas SJB submitted this information on the 11th of August. We saw that, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think that misstates the evidence. Ilijas submitted on the 5th. It was received on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You received the letter on the 11th of August.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That can be seen from the log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Pejic, before receiving a report from all SJBs in its territory, the CSB does not report to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not submit a full report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Or if it does submit a report, then it states in the report information not received from, and then what follows is the list of SJBs.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a partial or incomplete report can be filed. That's why I said in my answer to your first question not a full report. The centre could, and I suppose that the chief of the centre in this particular case really did that, namely, he sent a reply to the Ministry within the deadline but clearly state that it was -- the report was made based on available information, and to -- to justify their activity they will have enclosed dispatches sent out to the SJBs and stated that they -- that the replies are still pending. The chief of the centre had to at least inform the ministry that he was unable to collect the information in the said deadline. Otherwise, he would have been -- he may have been called to responsibility for failure to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the information from the SJB of Ilijas, once received by the CSB on the 11th of August, couldn't have made it to the MUP of the RS before that date; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the ministry of the RS, from the day this dispatch was sent out till the reception of incoming information, had to wait for at least ten days; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how far is Ilijas from Pale approximately as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think about 30 to 40 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, you said to Mr. Hannis while he was examining you that currently you were an inspector in the service for documenting war crimes.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a member of the team established by the MUP of the RS in 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us the official name of that team or that service of the MUP of the RS?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Team for investigating and documenting of criminal offences of war crimes of the MUP of the RS, established pursuant to the decision of the minister in 2005, as amended by subsequent amendments. Currently we -- this team works in the headquarters at Pale and is directly subordinate to the minister's office. It does operational work for the department of the police, and more precisely, the administration of the crime police. In all centres there are sub-teams, that is, departments and sections who -- that also do some work for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This investigates team which also documents war crimes is a body -- or the body that the Defence is -- Defence teams of the accused, including Mr. Stanisic, contact for documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes they do it directly, they approach the team directly, but some attorneys contact the ministry first, but in that case either the office of the director of the police or the office of the minister or the chief of the crime police administration forward their request to our team instructing us to act upon it and inform them what we have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So at any rate, this team for investigating and documenting war crimes is a body or administration within the MUP, the only such body that procures such documents and forwards it to the requesting party; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence this is the case, but the team doesn't have the entire documentation. So when requests are made for personal documents from personal files, we would forward that to our personnel administration and forward that directly to the applicant or go through the relevant body for investigating war crimes with the cabinet of the RS. That's the former government secretariat for co-operation with the ICTY. But the team would take care that all bodies of the MUP procure all available documents, integrate the documents and consult the -- consult the executive levels of the MUP and decide on the most appropriate way of transmitting the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking this because there have been some remarks by the Prosecution's with regard to the authenticity of the documents, some documents. I'll try to shorten that and focus on matters of interest to us, but we need your assistance for explaining this to the Trial Chamber. When a Defence team of one of the accused applies for some documents, you look for those documents or, rather, request these documents from the administration in charge in the MUP of the RS.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, unless we have that document already in our archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But if it's about a document that isn't in your archives but, rather, in one of the stations in the field, then that document is sent to you by that station.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then you inspect the document, copy it, and forward it to the applicant, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but first we consult the administration in charge and the minister's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if the Defence team of one of the accused from -- gets from the team for investigating and documenting war crimes of the RS a certain document, it's a fact that as soon as you forward that document to the Defence team that means that your team and the MUP do not doubt the authenticity of that document; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The authenticity of the documents, although they are copies, is corroborated by the fact that it was found in the archives of the MUP or one of its organisational units. Some documents that we provide are not stamped, and the copy doesn't show that it was certified, means that they were filed in the archives as copies. So these are not urgent documents that were indeed transmitted to someone and thus stamped, but, rather, a copy which is archived as such. Furthermore, I would like to say that -- well, possibly not in this case, but some attorneys without any need applies for a number of documents, documents that we have in our archives but in electronic form. These documents have been taken out by the investigators of the ICTY, assisted by the EUFOR. They have taken them out from the archives of the MUP and its organisational units. They brought them all here and scanned, and when they returned the documents to us, we got also electronic versions of the documents, and we use those in order to avoid searching the archives again, so that some documents could have been found more easily here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where are we going with this, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm just putting a question about the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, there has been numerous objections from Ms. Korner especially about the provenance of the documents, and when I gave the explanation that we received the document from the -- the team for investigation and documentation of the war crimes of the MUP of RS, Ms. Korner was actually suggesting that due to the fact that the document does not have the ERN number, there is -- there is -- there is a question of its authenticity and the existence of the original and alike. This is -- I found this as a -- as a good opportunity to clarify this situation, because this witness works at the -- he's inspector in this very same investigates and documentation team of MUP of RS. So we are getting the first-hand knowledge about that. That is the only reason why I raise this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions for this witness. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Pejic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just have a couple of questions because my learned friend Mr. Hannis, in his examination-in-chief, raised the issue about the Krajina CSB Banja Luka communications situation, so simply for that. Otherwise, I don't have any -- any other issue or question to raise with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pejic.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have a question to ask you on a topic broached by Mr. Hannis, and I would like through my questions to clarify the matter for Their Honours. Tell us, in the first several months, and let's say through to the end of 1992, you had information to the effect that the Krajina was almost fully encircled from north, south, east, and west. Of course, prior to the breaking through of the corridor. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In other words, the entire region was a battle-field of sorts; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was only in late June and early July as the corridor was made passable that physical links were restored, although they were not secure or stable in view of the narrowness of the corridor with the rest of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You had technical knowledge to that effect, and we had information that throughout 1992, in the region of the Krajina, there were dire problems with electricity supplies. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This -- because the very system on which the electricity supply was based on a grid, and, of course, certain transmission stations were required, just as is the case with the telecommunications system; is that not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that there was communication between the CSB Banja Luka and the municipal SJBs, but it was irregular and unreliable because, for instance, an SJB would have communication links with another SJB but not necessarily with all the others, and that was the volatile situation of the times, was it not?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm not really familiar with the situation with -- in the CSB Banja Luka because I wasn't there, but from what I was able to glean in the communications centre of the MUP and from what could be seen on the diagram, they were in a better position in terms of infrastructure than others, but I still know that we had to wait for several days before we would receive a signal in the communications centre of the MUP, that those in the CSB in Banja Luka had power and that we would be able to transmit the information we had to transmit. So I know that regardless of the infrastructure they had in place, the problems they were confronted with, especially in terms of power supplies, were dire. On some occasions we would wait for several days or even weeks in a row before we could manage to send out a dispatch. This particularly applied to the period of April and early May, at a time when I still worked in the communications centre of the MUP of RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In order to assist the Trial Chamber, you will recall and give us brief comments on it, although it was a long time ago, that precisely in this time period and because of the problems in power supplies and the blockade of communications, we have the sad anniversary of the death of several infants in the Banja Luka nursery hospital, precisely due to the power cuts.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I know that recently a memorial was erected in the memory of these infants. The problems were the result of the absence of any sort of communications. Had there been communication working at the time, appeals would not have been sent only to Belgrade for aid. And I was present at several such memorial services on the anniversaries of this tragic event.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Pejic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, how long do you think you would be in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think at least 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Because I'm thinking that although we're ten minutes in advance of the break, perhaps we should take the break a little early and then you can proceed without interruption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's -- that would be convenient for me. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we continue, I admit that we owe counsel and the parties an apology for not being clear as to when we were resuming. So you would have been waiting for us. You could have spent the extra ten minutes more usefully than just hanging around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pejic. I want to start --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to start with some of the matters that Mr. Zecevic raised this morning first, and then later on I'll go on to some things that he asked you about yesterday. At page 6, line 10 today, he asked you about the number of communications from the Sarajevo CSB in 1992 and mentioned the number of approximately 1.800. The -- the log-book you have there, P1428, we see that log-book was used in Vraca for the first 49 entries up to the 13th of May, and then the portion that begins for Sarajevo CSB, item number 1 there, I think is a date in June. I think it's the 14th of June. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Surely there must have been some dispatches sent and received during that time period between the 13th of May and 14th of June. Do you know where those would be recorded?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know with any certainty. It is possible that this part of -- that the dispatches in that period were transmitted from Kalovita Brda for the CSB, and the CSB itself did not need to have its own centre for as long as the two of us worked for both the MUP and the centre, but military records were not kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that last translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure if the witness said military or dual.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness said something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, the last part of your answer was that military records were not kept, but it's been suggested that what you actually said was that dual records were not kept. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned Kalovita Brda. Can you tell us again what that was and where it was?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a neighbourhood of Pale which bears the name. That's where another part of our centre was located, holding individuals who were preparing documents for encryption and other correspondence as well. It is possible that at the time when they were engaged in preparations to relocate the MUP from Vraca to Jahorina they transmitted dispatches from that centre. So it's possible that they have the relevant documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there was communications equipment located there as well in April and May of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the communications equipment was, the equipment that was being tested, as it were, and the equipment that was being prepared for the purposes of the communications centre and the security services communication centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that facility at Kalovita Brda one that is sometimes referred to as the Scout House or the Scouts' House?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which building it was, but some of these buildings were at one time used by scouts. That is true. Later on it was turned into a students' home, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you a document that I believe was dispatched during this time period, between 15 June and 14 -- between 13 May and 14 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Exhibit 1D46. And this was at tab 13 of my original selection for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Pejic, you'll see this is a document dated the 15 of May. Its reference number is 01-1/92, and it's an order from the minister creating war units. Did you -- did you see this document before? Did you see this in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly when I saw it, but I am -- I see that it's familiar, but I can't tell you whether I saw it back in May when it was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to the last page in both English and B/C/S, to the bottom. You'll see it's stamped and signed. Does that appear to be Mr. Stanisic's signature?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to the left side of the page at the bottom in B/C/S, please, we'll see it says "Forward to," the Presidency, the government, organisational units of the MUP and archives. So am I safe to assume that this document was something that would have been transmitted throughout the MUP?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I look at its contents I am familiar with them, but the document did not go through the communications centre. Judging by the reference number, I would say that it does not originate from the communications centre. Rather, I think that the order was sent out together with other regular mail from the minister's office. Those of us in the organisational units were made familiar or acquainted with this order by our superiors, that is to say, chiefs of the security services centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say it didn't go out to the communication centre, you mean the communication centre where you were working at Vraca in late April and early May?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's the centre I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you don't know whether or not it may have been sent out from Kalovita Brda.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't state with any certainty either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you indicated that you were aware of it. I will show you one place where you may have become aware of it. If we could look at Exhibit P160. This next one I want to show you, Mr. Pejic, is a summary of the meeting on 11 July 1992 in Belgrade. You attended that meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We actually see your name on the second page among those attending.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 15 of both the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the bottom half of the page, this is Mr. Stanisic speaking, at least that's who it's attributed to in this meeting, and in the last paragraph, my English translation says, beginning with the third sentence: "For that reason we passed a special order, number 01-1, dated 15/05 1992, in mid May, saying that the police be organised as well as other MUP services into war units." So at this meeting in Belgrade in July, that order that we just looked at was spoken about. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it possible given that date of 15 May and that number 01, is it possible that this was a new system of numbering starting from dispatches sent out from Kalovita Brda, because we see no further dispatches sent from Vraca after the 13th of May. So the timing is about right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This may be the case, or it may be the case that the log-book for orders, a new one was opened in the minister's office, or -- or in the office where they typed them out. I said that the order need not have necessarily been transmitted as a dispatch. It could have been distributed to the chiefs in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I want to go to page 7, line 21 today. Mr. Zecevic was asking you about some of the entries in P1428, the log-book that you have a hard copy of, and he was asking you about an entry, number 30, where it seemed to indicate that nothing had been sent to CSB Doboj. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you agreed that that would mean the dispatch was not transmitted. Would you allow for the possibility that another explanation could be that the communication worker on duty may have indeed sent it later but failed to make an entry in the log-book, because he was busy doing other things or a shift change? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 2100 hours or after the time these other dispatches were transmitted, during the hand-over of duty, the communications officer is duty-bound to inform the colleague replacing him fully of the dispatches that were sent or still remained to be sent. Thus the communications officer taking up duties would contact Doboj, transmit the message and do the same thing that his colleague who was there previously did, would make an entry, or if he failed to transmit the dispatch, he would have to contact a courier to come and pick it up, but a note would have been made to that effect as well. In this case, evidently the communications officer did not transmit the dispatch from the centre. If it had been the case that you were referring to, then it would have been a failure on the part of the communications officer to transmit it and a note of this would have to have been made in the record during the hand-over of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in fairness to the communication workers who were available at the time, as I understand it, it was only you and Obrad Trifkovic. So there were only two of you doing all the work for the centre, 24 hours a day, seven days a week, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this instant example it's my handwriting, but you can see that my signature is absent from where "Doboj" is written. And Trifkovic would have made an entry, because he was an officer with more experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you then -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is not what the witness said. What was recorded was not what the witness said about Trifkovic. Can you please -- I mean, I can -- I can say what the witness said and maybe he can confirm, but I don't thing that you would be happy with that, Mr. Hannis, so please clarify that or we ask for a verification request.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Pejic, it's been suggested by my learned friend that what's in the transcript is not what you said. Let me read what's in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it the entire thing or just the last sentence, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It appears that the question and answer have been conflated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. It wasn't recorded properly the answer of the witness. The witness said something different in his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last sentence --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Line 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last sentence, Mr. Pejic, is -- your answer is translated as: "And Trifkovic would have made an entry because he was an officer with more experience." Was that what you said, and if not, can you say now what you previously said?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the gist is as follows: I said that had Trifkovic transmitted the dispatch, he would have made an entry to that effect, because he is a colleague who had more experience than me. In my view, he could not have committed such an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Pejic, surely even an experienced professional can make a mistake or an omission.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to object to this. This is calling for speculation. The question was put and the witness answered what is it in his opinion the situation about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he gave an answer, I think, which I'm entitled to question, and I think the question I asked is an appropriate one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you saying professionals do not make mistakes? Especially in the stress of the first few weeks of a war when you're working 24-hour shifts with only one other colleague to handle all the communications work?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I would approach your question in a slightly different manner than the way Mr. Zecevic formulated his objection in that as it is now phrased, it appears that you're arguing with the witness. Perhaps you can make your point in a different way by rephrasing your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I think my first question was appropriately phrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility that even an experienced professional can make a mistake or an omission?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is that every living person can make a mistake. You, just as me and anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you look at the CSB section of the hard copy for the entries number 68, 69, and 73, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If Your Honours still have your hard copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see, those appear to be blank. Can you -- can you tell us what that means or how at that came to be?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. When somebody's preparing a dispatch, if he doesn't want to enter his own registration number, that is the number that comes in front of the serial number, he can call the communications number and ask which the following number of dispatch is. In this particular case, it was said that the following number was 68. However, in the meantime, the author who received that number gave up on writing the dispatch and that's why it was left blank. So the number was taken, but the dispatch was never made or transmitted to the communications centre for distribution. It could have been the chief of the department of the police or of the crime police or anybody else, and that's why it's blank. If the dispatch had actually come in, it would have been entered under this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Mr. Hannis. I think for the -- for the clarity of the record, we should enter the P number of the document you were referring to when you posed the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The log-book is P1428.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: P1428. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pejic, sticking with P1428, I have a few more questions. Mr. Zecevic, at page 8, line 12, today was asking you about entries 47 and 48, and you'll see there are a list of addressees there which include Doboj and Trebinje, but it appears that nothing was sent to them because there's no phone number entered as there is for the Sarajevo, Banja Luka, and Bijeljina CSBs. Then he asked you if you would agree with him that this means communication lines with the centres in Doboj and Trebinje were nonexistent at this time and you said yes. My question is related to that, and could you look at entry number 11 in P1428. This is dated 26 April 1992, number 25, decision returned. It lists the five CSBs. There are five telephone numbers, and there are several signatures in the far right column. So it appears -- am I correct in assuming that on the 26th of April there was a phone line or there was a connection between Doboj and Trebinje and this item was sent to them on that day?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For Trebinje the answer is yes, but for Doboj no, because there are no -- the number is not initialled, and in the last column there is a line for the "sent" entry. You can see that the other towns have this data entered but not Doboj, because there are five signatures of the signalsmen and this one is not marked as sent, but Trebinje is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you then look at number 13 and 15, which are both entries signed by you. Can you tell me whether or not these entries indicate that the subject documents were sent to both Trebinje and Doboj on the --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 26th of April at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the second one on the 27th of April, item number 15?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. So prior to May 11th, when we see the entries for items 47 and 48, prior to that there had been communication lines with Doboj and Trebinje. Do you know when that changed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beware when we're speaking about communications, which I explained at the beginning, especially when your colleague asked me about Banja Luka, it can happen that you have the line at 7.00 in the morning but you don't at 1900. So we would wait for Banja Luka to contact us so that we can send them something. It was the same with Doboj and Trebinje. The situation changed on an hourly basis: Now you have a phone line. Now you don't have it. Sometimes it was because of Trebinje or Doboj, but sometimes even we, at Vraca, would be left without electricity, and then we would be unable to send anything, although they were able to receive. So in the morning the situation would be different from that in the afternoon, and this went on day by day. So there's nothing unusual with dispatches being able to be sent one day but not on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask a couple of questions about the last subject matter Mr. Zecevic brought up today. He asked you about your current work, and the documents that you get which are sometimes given out to requesters, and it relates to the authenticity of documents. The documents you have in the collections where you work now with the team that you work with, as I understood your answer, those were documents that were found in the archives of various organisational units within the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some of them. We mostly have documents that have already been here in The Hague, and they mostly have an electronic version too. Part of the documents we collect from the various administrations in charge through the administration of the police or the minister's office. When we get the documents, we make the sets complete, and we send them to the applicants, and we act in the same manner when we get requests from the Prosecution. Not only this one but also other Prosecution -- Prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. On behalf of this Prosecution, we appreciate that. My question is concerning your source materials from archives in the organisational units, it seemed to me that those documents could include documents that were placed there by individuals, former employees of the MUP, maybe even current employees of the MUP, who may have been suspects in this Tribunal or state court or had a motivation. That's one possibility, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we look for documents, we look for them in the official archives of the MUP, and you were able to see that these documents have their register numbers, and as a rule, they must have been archived then. This document, the activity report for nine months, has an electronic version too. And most of the other documents were copies that had to be sent to the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour, I believe perhaps when the witness leaves or is excused we would need a clarification on the position of the Office of the Prosecutor concerning the last question Mr. Hannis posed, because it was my understanding that the Office of the Prosecutor is using the very same documents which were sized -- seized, I'm sorry, seized in the archives of the RS MUP or CSBs or SJBs. Therefore, if the Prosecution's position is that these documents in the archives are the documents which were, as I see from his question, planted by some of the -- some accused or other individuals, then we would need a clarification on the exact position of the -- of the Office of the Prosecutor in respect to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Our position on documents will be related to particular documents. I wasn't here for some of the objections that Mr. Zecevic has referred to as being made by Ms. Korner to particular documents. It's my understanding that we have had some documents that don't have stamps, don't have signatures. In some cases I think one document we objected to was a document that appeared to be -- was purported to be from the SDA. Now, if I am getting this mixed up with something else. But we do have a question. For example, an informant for State Security Service may provide documents to State Security Service that purport to be from the SDA. Yeah, we may have an issue about whether that's an authentic document. The mere fact that it is in the RS MUP archives doesn't automatically make it authentic, just as a document in the OTP collection doesn't automatically make it authentic. We have to examine each one individually. That's why I'm asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on. Not something I need to argue with you, Mr. Pejic. It's for us lawyers, I think, to talk about. Let me now go to yesterday. Mr. Zecevic asked you, at page 12166 going on to 12167, about the requirement for security-related events to be reported up the chain, and you explained how before the war even minor things like stopping an individual and asking for his identification was something that would be reported, but I understood from your answer that that kind of thing wasn't done during the war. Those things weren't being reported by dispatch, were they, how many times a policeman stopped someone to see their ID?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mentioned in the bulletin of daily events as statistical information. If the person was not apprehended and deprived of liberty, writing a dispatch would not be necessary. It would only be recorded in the statistical section of the daily bulletin. But in war that certainly wasn't possible. Also, given the fact that the police officers on duty didn't always -- weren't always able to communicate with the duty shift officer because we didn't have enough portable radio stations. So they were only able to report on that when they returned from their duty shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in terms of the kinds of things that were sent by dispatch before the war but which were not commonly sent by dispatch during the war, I -- I understood that, for example, in 1991 by dispatch would be sent things such as all points bulletins to be on the lookout for a particular individual, or notices of appointment concerning employment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first part, yes, but even the second. All official correspondence in peacetime which is -- which doesn't abound in information contained could be sent by dispatch and was. So this also applied to wanted notices and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But I understood that during war time, and we don't seem to see examples of those kind of things, notices of appointment or wanted notices being sent by dispatch in 1992 after April 6th.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They -- that wasn't done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 12170, line 11, Mr. Zecevic and you were discussing the number of dispatches sent out pre-war, and he said: "If I were to tell you that it would be logical to expect the number of dispatches during war time, the total number of dispatches, should increase by 30 per cent, would you agree?" And your answer was: "In these," there's a question mark in my transcript, I think this was probably "in these circumstances," or "in these realm of security and security-related events, yes." Now, with regard to this figure of 300.000 dispatches that was mentioned as being a yearly figure for the pre-war MUP, what percentage of 300.000 dispatches were security related? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise figure, but certainly most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what percentage would be those things like notices of appointment and non-security-related matters? Any percentage you can give us?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the exact percentage, but a very small number of dispatches had to do with personnel matters. In urgent cases when the minister appoints the commander of a police station, then the personnel service would send out a dispatch to inform the others, but -- and they would also state that the decision would follow by regular mail. Such dispatches were -- there were much fewer of them than dispatches of operational character.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the first time that you ever heard this number of 30 per cent as being a likely increase to expect when war broke out? Had you seen that or read that some place, or was when Mr. Zecevic asked you the question the first time you heard 30 per cent?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was then that I heard this figure of 30 per cent for the first time. I agreed that it was to be expected, that the number of operator dispatches rise by at least that percentage. The expected percentage may actually be greater than that, but if I wanted a more realistic estimate, then I would have to say that it has to be viewed from the perspective of the events that were happening. Things were happening very fast, especially the movements of population and the start of combat activities and so on. Why am I not insisting on a greater percentage? Because even though the war was starting, the number of criminal offences such as brawls and so on, that usually would take up much more of the dispatch communication was reduced. That seems illogical but that was the case. As far as I remember, theft and breaking into houses were -- became more common, more numerous then, and due to that, the number of dispatches had to increase in this operational aspect, the policing aspect which was security relevant. Whether that percentage is 30 per cent or not, in some it was below that, in some it was greater, especially in urban settlements. But I cannot go into a deeper analysis of the situation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. My question stems in part from the fact that you worked in analysis in your professional career, and I'm just trying to find out if there was some kind of science that was applied to come up with this estimate, because before 1992, neither you nor anybody else in the MUP had the experience of what it would be like to run a communications system in the MUP, in Bosnia, in war-time circumstances. So where's 30 per cent come from? Why not 10? Why not 99? Why not -15? I just don't understand how that number can be picked out. Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did point out that for a more precise estimate I would need an analysis of the overall events in the area, but as I don't have one, I did not oppose what the attorney put to me, because I didn't have a foundation to do that, nor did he say anything which I would spontaneously oppose. For example, for the area of Ilidza, in the first seven days, the numbers of -- the number of dispatches about attacks on persons and the facilities should have been much greater than was really done. That's why I said that it was realistic to expect a much greater number of dispatches containing security-relevant information and security-relevant events. And this other aspect about which you spoke, I'm not saying that it did not drop, because the entire documentation, all the log-books, remained in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I guess I need to make sure we're starting from the right -- the right base in trying to examine these numbers that Mr. Zecevic talked about. If you could take a quick look at Exhibit P625. This was at tab 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the annual report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic showed you one page from this report. I'm going to start with page number 23 in the English. It's page 32, I believe, in e-court, in the B/C/S. And I will tell you, Mr. Pejic, that this page is in the section under II, "Other task of the Ministry," item number 1, reporting and informing, and the paragraph you saw before was the one that says -- it's the next-to-last paragraph in your B/C/S. It says: "On average, 15 dispatches a day were sent to the centres and other organs of the interior from the MUP headquarters (a total of 4170) and on average 16 a day were received, a total of 4400." Now, if you can keep those numbers in mind, 4.170 and 4.400. I'd like to direct you to another page within the same annual report. This is page 37 in the B/C/S and page 27 of the English. And this paragraph I'm going to show you now, Mr. Pejic, it comes from a section of the report, number 3, task and duties of communications and cryptographic data protection. And --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it. I think that it was on the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I need the electronic page 37 in the B/C/S, which has a different page number because of the cover page. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the very bottom of the page on the right there, you'll see it says: "In this period for the needs of the MUP headquarters, 2969 open dispatches were sent and 2802 were received; 1300 closed dispatches were sent and 1601 received." If my math is correct, I count 4.269 sent instead of 4.170. Does that mean there's two different kinds of dispatches and the total number really should be somewhere in the neighbourhood of 8.300 sent? Because this is the same report for MUP headquarters, but this relates specifically to the cryptographic data protection section. Do you know why there's that discrepancy? Because if they're talking about the total number of dispatches for MUP headquarters, it seems like it should be identical to that 4.170 number we saw before, unless there's two different kinds of dispatches we're talking about. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number you're referring to now is contained in the earlier sum total, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, the author of the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me stop you there. This number is higher than the previous number. The other number was 4.170 sent, and this is 4.269. So I don't see how this number could be contained within the lower number. Do you follow me?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we're looking at different figures. In this period, for the purposes of the MUP, the seat, 2.969 were sent out, and 2.802 were received. Earlier on where the total figure appeared, it was much higher than this one, and the explanation is quite simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. Wait. Wait. Let me stop you. Maybe there's a problem with my English translation, but 2.969 is the number of open dispatches sent, and 1.300 is the number of closed, so that makes a total of 4.269 sent. That's combining both open and closed. Is my English translation correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that number 4.269 is almost 100 higher than the number we saw previously at the earlier page in your report of 4.170.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the translation you have is wrong. In the Serbian version the numbers are smaller, and I can account for this by the fact that the report presents, through communications statistics, the activity of the organisational units in the seat of the MUP, i.e., in the administrations. The other number, the first number of more than 4.000 that's mentioned, also encompasses some of the activities in the centres. The figure which appears at page 33 of the report does not include these dispatches too. It only includes the dispatches of the MUP in the seat, that's to say, the administration of the crime police, the administration of ordinary police, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The page you're looking at right now says 2.969 dispatches, open dispatches, sent, and 1.300 closed sent for the needs of MUP headquarters, right? We agree with that so far?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you add those two together and they come up with 4.269 total dispatches sent during this period for the needs of MUP headquarters. Right? Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go back to e-court page number 32 in the B/C/S and page 23 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Pejic. I'm just trying to be sure I understand this. What my English translation says here is that from the MUP headquarters, a total of 4.170 dispatches in all lines of work were sent to the centres and other organs of the interior. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So can you explain the difference between those two numbers? Does this mean there's 4.170 from MUP headquarters and also 4.269 and the total should be something 8400? Or is it just a mistake or do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that when it came to the earlier figure a dispatch was counted twice. As for the sum total of 4.170, I think it's correct, because it's taken over from the log-book. As for the dispatches transmitted from the seat of the MUP, that is to say, from the administrations, a dispatch that -- a dispatch may have been recorded twice because it appeared in two administrations, although the more reliable data is contained in the communications centre, because that's where all these dispatches converge and where they confer numbers on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Be -- be that as it may, whatever the number is, I want to ask you about some of the possible reasons that there was a significant decrease in the number of dispatches sent is during the war time, and I'll list some things and ask if you agree that that could be one reason dispatches went down. For one thing, the 300.000 number was -- pre-war, that was the entire Bosnia when there were, I don't know, twice as many stations for the entire MUP versus how many stations you had in the RS MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN PEJIC [Resumed]
